Spectacle
SPEK-ta-kl
n. (a show; something exhibited to be looked at)
Greek theatron, a theatre, and so what is displayed in one — the root of the English theatre. Latin spectaculum, a show, from spectare, to look at. Paul's image is the arena, where the condemned were brought out last.

Biblical Definition

For I think that God hath set forth us the apostles last, as it were appointed to death: for we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men. The image is the Roman arena and the detail is exact. The condemned were brought out last, at the end of the day's programme, to die in front of a crowd that had been entertained by everything preceding. Paul says the apostles occupy that slot, and he says God has set them there. The Corinthians were preoccupied with status, with eloquence, with which teacher they belonged to, and Paul answers with a deliberately humiliating comparison in the verses that follow: we are fools for Christ's sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong; ye are honourable, but we are despised. He then drops the irony and simply describes the conditions — even unto this present hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace — ending with: we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day. The word spectacle also reaches further than the human audience. The apostles are a show to angels as well as men, which is the same thought Peter expresses when he says the angels desire to look into these things. What is being publicly exhibited in the sufferings of Christ's servants is watched by more than the crowd in the seats.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a show; something exhibited to view; something presented to the sight or notice, usually of an extraordinary kind.

expand to see more

SPECTACLE, n. A show; something exhibited to view; usually, something presented to view as extraordinary, or as worthy of special notice.

SPECTACLE, n. Anything presented to the view, particularly anything that strikes with astonishment.

THEATRE, n. A house or edifice appropriated to the representation of dramatic spectacles; a place of exhibition.

OFFSCOURING, n. That which is scoured off; hence, refuse; recrement; anything vile and despised.

APOSTLE, n. A person deputed to execute some important business; but appropriately, a disciple of Christ commissioned to preach the gospel.

Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 4:9 — "For I think that God hath set forth us the apostles last, as it were appointed to death: for we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men."

1 Corinthians 4:10 — "We are fools for Christ's sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong; ye are honourable, but we are despised."

1 Corinthians 4:11 — "Even unto this present hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace;"

1 Corinthians 4:13 — "Being defamed, we intreat: we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day."

Modern Corruption

Christian ministry is widely modelled on platform, influence, and reputation; Paul locates apostolic ministry in the arena's last slot and says God put it there.

expand to see more

The celebrity model of ministry — the conference circuit, the personal brand, the platform measured in followers — is the Corinthian error with better technology. That church wanted teachers who reflected well on them, and Paul's response was to describe himself as a condemned man brought out last for the crowd's amusement, hungry, beaten, and homeless. The comparison is not false modesty; it is a direct attack on the metric. A ministry evaluated by reach and reputation is being evaluated by the standard Paul is dismantling, and the New Testament offers no apostle who would have scored well.

The prosperity teaching sharpens the contradiction to a point, since it holds that the King's servants should be visibly prospering and that hardship indicates deficient faith. 1 Corinthians 4 is written by the apostle to the Gentiles about his own settled condition — even unto this present hour — and he attributes the arrangement to God: God hath set forth us the apostles last. The comfort in the passage is real and is available to any faithful servant in obscurity or disgrace. The seats are not the only audience. The spectacle is played before angels, and the verdict that matters is given by the Lord, who Paul says will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of the hearts.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek theatron (G2302), a theatre or spectacle; epithanatios (G1935), appointed to death; perikatharma (G4027), filth or refuse; peripsema (G4067), offscouring.

expand to see more

Greek theatron (G2302) — a theatre, and so a public show; rendered spectacle.

Greek epithanatios (G1935) — condemned to death; rendered appointed to death, its only occurrence.

Greek perikatharma (G4027) — what is scraped off in cleansing; rendered filth of the world.

Greek peripsema (G4067) — scrapings, offscouring; the lowest term Paul could find.

Greek apostolos (G652) — one sent with a commission; the office being described.

Usage

"“we are made a spectacle unto the world” — the arena's last slot."

"“God hath set forth us the apostles last” — the arrangement attributed to God."

"“the offscouring of all things” — the lowest word available."
